Every Star is Alive

Genre: Physics puzzle · Micro-action · Minimal arcade
Hook: One-finger control with readable, tangible gravity.
Instant feedback loop: Approach → capture → becomes an orbital ally → score. Moving hazards and a portal create a tight collect → exit loop.

Overview

This game is about — steer a living star with your mouse, harness gravity to capture wandering micro-stars into your orbit, dodge moving hazards, and step through the portal once you’ve met the score goal.

  • Core loop: Scout the scene → slow in & capture stars → grow your orbit & score → reach the quota → enter the portal → next level.
  • Platform: PC (Unity 2D).
  • Audience: Players who enjoy physical feedback, light strategy, and short-session challenges.

flowchart TD A[Scout the scene] –> B[Approach a star] B –> C{Capture?} C –>|Yes| D[Becomes orbital ally] C –>|No| B D –> E[Orbit grows & score+1] E –> F{Quota met?} F –>|Yes| G[Enter Portal -> Next Level] F –>|No| A

Download & Trailer

  • ▶️ Trailer: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_t_BWbHAO74
  • 🎮 Play / Download: https://geraaer.itch.io/everystar-is-alive

Physics & Gravity (System You Can Feel)

Gravity sources:

  • Player (controllable star): has mass and a circular interaction radius (capture zone).
  • Captor (scene gravity body): static source with its own interaction radius.
  • Affected bodies: Star (free-flying micro-stars).

Gravity model: For each gravity source, apply acceleration with an inverse-square falloff; integrate velocity with clamping by maxVelocity.

  • Accumulate contributions from all active sources each frame.
  • Position clamp inside screen; damping on player acceleration to keep motion readable.
  • Orbiting satellites space out using orbitSpacing; angular speed tuned for circular readability.

Controls (Simple & Intuitive)

  • Mouse move: The player star accelerates toward the cursor with capped speed and soft damping; position is clamped inside the screen.
  • Hotkeys:
    • R — Restart the current level (resets time scale).
    • N — Skip to next level (debug/demo).
    • K / L — Toggle mouse cursor visibility (presentation or immersion).

Gameplay & Mechanics

Orbiting

  • On capture, a star becomes a satellite: enable trail, switch collider to trigger, and add score.
  • Assign an orbit radius; multiple satellites auto-space via orbitSpacing.

Capture test

  • When a Star enters a source’s interaction radius and its relative speed/heading indicates it cannot escape (escape-speed and direction thresholds), it becomes that source’s satellite.

flowchart TD S[Star enters interaction radius] –> V{Relative speed < v_escape?} V –>|Yes| H{Heading within capture cone?} V –>|No| R[Deflect / continue free-fly] H –>|Yes| O[Assign orbit radius & phase] H –>|No| R O –> T[Enable trail, set trigger collider] T –> P[Score +1; add to satellites list]

Level & Difficulty Design

Building Blocks

  • Terrain/Hazards: Barriers moving back-and-forth between endpoints; speed and path editable.
  • Goals: TotalScore (exit threshold), placement of Pickups, number and initial speed range of Stars.
  • Risk knobs: Screen-edge bounces (with damping), hazard collisions, multi-source gravity tug-of-war.
  • Exit: Portal.

Scoring, Win/Loss, Objectives

  • Scoring: Pickups convert into orbiting companions around the player by dynamically adding OrbitAroundTarget; grants Score+1 with immediate visual feedback. Stars captured by the player also score via LevelManager (per level rules).
  • Win: Enter the Portal when Score ≥ totalScore; play win SFX, pause time, and show WinTip.
  • Loss: Colliding Player or Star with Barriers triggers a sprite-based explosion, pauses time, shows LoseTip, and plays the fail SFX.
Intro: Fixed hazards + few Pickups; a handful of slow, nearby Stars. Establish approach → capture → orbit mental model quickly.
Intermediate: Add one or two Captor sources and asynchronous moving Barriers; players must time entries during favorable relative-velocity windows.
Challenge: Faster Stars, narrow corridors of Barriers, and angled Portal placement; emphasizes pacing and route planning.

Game Scene

UI / UX Design

  • VFX: LevelManager.Explode() plays a multi-frame explosion on the Effect sorting layer.
  • Audio:
    • BGM: started via Game Manager / Audio Manager.
    • SFX: PlayWinSound() / PlayLoseSound(); add a light capture SFX for clarity.
  • Style: Minimal sci-fi; geometric shapes with neon trails. BG.cs loops background sprites as a slow parallax-like frame cycle.

1. Overview

A cozy café game combining time management, dual-character perspective, and resource strategy.

Tulips Café is a simulation game that merges elements of time management, resource management, and dual perspective game play.

The game features two primary playable characters: Anne, the café owner who handles resources and strategy,

Jessica, the waitress who manages orders, customer interactions, and dish preparations. The player switches between both characters to optimize the café’s operations while interacting with a diverse set of customer witches.

Anne and Jessica

2. Gameplay & Mechanics

tips

Core Gameplay Loop:

Switching Perspectives:

The player can switch between Anne and Jessica. Each character has distinct responsibilities and tasks:

Anne: Manages resources, unlock new dishes and researches recipes. Jessica: Fulfill orders, serves dishes and interacts with customers The switch consumes Action Points(AP),which are limited each day. This mechanic forces players to prioritize tasks and make strategic decisions on when to switch between the characters.

Resource Management:

Essence: A magical resource used to unlock new recipes and upgrade the café’s offerings.

Gold: A more mundane resource used for daily purchases like Essence and upgrades.

Reputation: Gained by serving all the delivery orders and witches within today.

If your Reputation is high, the witches are more likely to visit your café, which means you are more likely to get more money. Be aware that the frequent visit of witches may cause you don’t have enough AP to complete all the orders, which means your reputation will drop.

In the early development stages, a Python-based version of this game was built to emulate the core gameplay loops and optimize the game’s parameters. The use of AI allowed us to make data-driven decisions about the game’s economy and mechanics, ensuring that the progression curve is challenging but fair for players. The AI simulations provided a foundation for future updates and expansions, allowing the design to evolve and scale. Overview

Throng: Evolution is a single-player simulation/strategy game focused on guiding a population of creatures through the pressures of survival and evolution. The player鈥檚 role can be described as part observer, part 鈥渘ature custodian.鈥?Rather than directly controlling individual creatures, the player influences the environment and initial conditions, then watches natural selection play out and can intervene strategically. The experience is somewhat akin to being an ecologist running an experiment or a deity overseeing a small ecosystem.

Target Audience

Middle to high school biology students, and the general public interested in science education.

Learning Outcomes:

  • Understand the mechanism of natural selection and how environmental pressures affect which individuals survive and reproduce.
  • Recognize that 鈥渟urvival of the fittest鈥?refers to being best suited to an environment 鈥?not merely the biggest or strongest 鈥?and that even less 鈥渟trong鈥?individuals can survive better if they require fewer resources or blend into the environment more effectively.

Background&Reseasrch

Natural selection is a cornerstone of biology, yet numerous studies show it is widely misunderstood[3]. Many students 鈥?even some with biology education 鈥?struggle to grasp how evolution by natural selection truly works[3]. Misconceptions are the norm, and a solid understanding of natural selection is 鈥渢he rare exception鈥漑4]. One prevalent misunderstanding is the idea that 鈥渇ittest鈥?means the strongest or fastest individual. In reality, evolutionary 鈥渇itness鈥?means being best suited to survive and reproduce in a given environment. As science educators note, 鈥渢he fittest really is the 鈥榞ood enough.鈥?As long as you get a chance to reproduce and pass on your genes, you win.鈥漑1]. In other words, an organism that survives long enough to reproduce is 鈥渇it,鈥?even if it isn鈥檛 the biggest or strongest. This serious game directly addresses that misconception by demonstrating scenarios where, for example, smaller or slower creatures might survive better if they require fewer resources or blend into the environment more effectively.

Fundamentally, Darwin鈥檚 theory of natural selection was built on a few key observations about populations. Organisms have the potential to reproduce exponentially, leading to huge population growth in principle[5]. However, in nature we do not see unlimited growth; populations tend to stabilize because resources (food, space, etc.) are limited. Darwin described how most offspring do not survive to reproduce, due to starvation, predation, disease, and competition 鈥?thus population sizes remain roughly stable over time[2]. This imbalance between the capacity for exponential growth and the reality of limited resources creates a 鈥渟truggle for existence鈥漑6]. In Throng: Evolution, this principle is built into the simulation: creatures produce offspring, but only a fraction can survive given the food available, illustrating concepts of carrying capacity and population dynamics. By including these elements, the game connects ecological constraints to evolutionary outcomes, reinforcing why survival of the fittest emerges naturally from competition over resources.

Educational research suggests that active learning and simulations can improve understanding of complex scientific concepts. Traditional teaching about evolution often struggles to correct ingrained misconceptions, but learning-by-doing offers promise. Hands-on games and simulations have been used to demonstrate natural selection in classrooms with success[7]. For example, simple analog games (like card or board games) have helped students experience how selection works by 鈥渂reeding鈥?or removing individuals based on traits[7]. In a more technology-driven approach, interactive simulations allow learners to manipulate variables and see evolutionary processes unfold in real-time. One project by Cignoni et al. (2015) developed a digital predator鈥損rey ecosystem where 鈥渢he game lets the player modify the fundamental parameters of the species and observe the evolution of the ecosystem.鈥?The player could even intervene to add or remove individuals, experimenting with how the system balances out[8]. This kind of inquiry-based exploration aligns with modern educational strategies that emphasize learning through experimentation and observation.

Serious games have been shown to enhance student motivation, which is important for learning[9][11]. However, research also notes that the impact on achievement (test scores) can vary[10]. Some studies suggest that games, on their own, may not always boost achievement as much as more traditional methods; yet they can significantly increase interest, time-on-task, and the willingness to engage with difficult material. A balanced approach 鈥?such as integrating games with discussions, reflection questions, or quizzes 鈥?could combine the best of both worlds[10]. Throng: Evolution is designed with this balance in mind. It includes real-time feedback (like charts and tooltips that interpret what is happening using scientific vocabulary), which can be used in classrooms to prompt discussion and reflection.

Game Scene

Building on these insights, Throng: Evolution is designed as a serious game 鈥?a game with an explicit educational purpose. Unlike entertainment-only games, serious games are defined by their learning objectives (in this case, teaching natural selection)[9]. Research shows that well-designed serious games can indeed enhance student engagement, motivation, and even behavior toward learning[9]. By immersing players in a dynamic model of evolution, the game aims to leverage curiosity and interactivity to deepen understanding. Moreover, because players can directly see the consequences of changes (like a shift in available food or a mutation in traits), they can correct their misconceptions through visual feedback and experimentation.

Concept Game Mapping
Population size N Number of living Thronglets
Growth rate r dN/dt, displayed live
Carrying capacity K Derived from total food
Mutation 卤5-10 % random variation
Selection pressure Resource scarcity / energy cost

Using a game-based approach for teaching evolution offers several potential advantages. Engagement and Motivation: Students are typically more engaged when learning feels like playing. Studies have found that gamified lessons and serious games significantly boost student motivation[10]. In the context of evolution (often considered a dry or abstract topic by learners), a game can spark interest and encourage students to spend more time thinking about evolutionary processes. The interactive nature of Throng: Evolution means learners are not just reading about natural selection 鈥?they are actively doing it, guiding a population through challenges. This active involvement can lead to better retention of concepts, as players form personal experiences with the material.

Educational Rationale

To ensure that learning objectives remain the focus, the game鈥檚 interface emphasizes meaningful data: population size (N), growth rates (dN/dt), carrying capacity estimates (K), and basic trait averages (e.g. speed, lifespan, metabolism). When these values change in response to player interventions (e.g. reducing food), it creates teachable moments without requiring long textual explanations. The combination of visual feedback and strategic knobs mirrors the practice of scientific investigation 鈥?asking, 鈥淲hat if we change X? Why did Y result?鈥?鈥?and then checking results via charts. This style of experiential learning can be especially helpful in countering misconceptions, since players may discover that outcomes conflict with their initial beliefs. If a player assumes the fastest creatures will always do best, a scarcity scenario might produce the opposite conclusion because of metabolic costs. Such 鈥減roductive failures鈥?can be powerful in reshaping understanding[3][4].

Game Scene

Learning-by-doing also supports the development of 鈥渟ystems thinking,鈥?a crucial skill for understanding biology. The concepts of population dynamics, competition, and ecological equilibrium involve feedback loops (e.g., more predators reduce prey; fewer prey starving leads to fewer predators), delays (changes accumulating over time), and trade-offs (such as speed vs. energy consumption). By interacting with a simulated ecosystem, players deepen their grasp of these system-level dynamics. According to classroom experience and educational theory, increased engagement plus hands-on involvement can lead to better retention of concepts, as players form personal experiences with the material.

Visualization of Abstract Concepts: Evolution can be hard to grasp because it occurs over long timescales and involves statistical outcomes. A simulation speeds up time and lets players visualize abstract concepts like genetic variation, differential survival, and population change. For instance, rather than merely hearing that variation in a trait can confer a survival advantage, players will see that advantage play out (e.g. creatures with a certain trait surviving a famine). This aligns with the pedagogical idea that concrete experiences can solidify understanding of theoretical concepts.

Addressing Misconceptions through Exploration: Misconceptions such as 鈥渟trength equals fitness鈥?or 鈥渋ndividuals evolve on purpose鈥?can be corrected by letting players test and observe. In the game, if a player assumes only the fastest creatures will thrive, they might be surprised to find that in a scarce food scenario, the fastest (but high-metabolism) creatures actually starve, whereas slower, low-metabolism ones survive longer. Such outcomes directly confront prior assumptions, providing teachable moments. The game鈥檚 design includes on-screen feedback cues and explanations (described later) to explicitly point out these outcomes, helping players connect the simulation events to real-world evolutionary principles.

鈥he evolutionary 鈥済ame of survival,鈥?students and players can learn-by-doing in a way that textbooks or lectures cannot easily replicate. The following sections detail the design of the game, including its core mechanics and how they map to educational concepts.

Literature-Informed Design: Our approach is informed by findings in educational research. Serious games can improve learning experiences, but they must be carefully designed to maintain focus on learning goals. One concern researchers note is that students may get 鈥渙verly focused on playing the educational games rather than learning from them.鈥漑11] In light of this, Throng: Evolution incorporates features to keep the educational content front-and-center. For example, the game provides real-time data displays and 鈥渢eaching tips鈥?pop-ups that interpret what is happening in educational terms (such as noting when the population reaches a stable size, linking it to carrying capacity). By explicitly connecting gameplay events to scientific terminology and concepts, we aim to prevent the game from being a mindless exercise. Additionally, while games can boost motivation, some studies have shown mixed results on whether they boost achievement (knowledge gains) as much as traditional teaching[10]. To maximize learning, Throng: Evolution could be used alongside reflection activities: for instance, students might be prompted to predict outcomes, explain results, or answer quiz questions after gameplay. This blended approach leverages the engagement of the game and the rigor of traditional assessment to ensure both motivation and learning outcomes are high[10]. In summary, the rationale for Throng: Evolution is to provide an engaging, research-backed learning tool that makes the principles of natural selection intuitive. By simulating the evolutionary 鈥済ame of survival,鈥?students and players can learn-by-doing in a way that textbooks or lectures cannot easily replicate. The following sections detail the design of the game, including its core mechanics and how they map to educational concepts.

Game Concept

Throng: Evolution is a single-player simulation/strategy game focused on guiding a population of creatures through the pressures of survival and evolution. The player鈥檚 role can be described as part observer, part 鈥渘ature custodian.鈥?Rather than directly controlling individual creatures, the player influences the environment and initial conditions, then watches natural selection play out and can intervene strategically. The experience is somewhat akin to being an ecologist running an experiment or a deity overseeing a small ecosystem.

Game Scene

Game World & Scenario: The game is set in a simplified ecosystem represented in 2D. The core scenario centers on a species of small creatures (the 鈥渢hronglets鈥? that must gather food, survive, and reproduce. There are no humanoid characters 鈥?the focus is on the creatures (and possibly predators or other factors in extended scenarios). Each round or session of the game represents several generations of these creatures. The environment contains resource patches (food sources) that the creatures need to consume to gain energy. Over time, resources can be depleted and regrow, and the environment can change (through player actions,). The visual style is clear and functional 鈥?creatures might be represented by simple shapes or icons with different colors or sizes indicating their traits, and resource patches are identifiable spots on the map.

Game Scene

Gameplay Loop

The high-level loop of Throng: Evolution is: Set up conditions -> Run simulation (creatures live, breed, die) -> Observe outcomes -> (Optional) intervene or adjust -> Next generation evolves -> Outcome/feedback. During the simulation phase, creatures autonomously move, eat, and reproduce according to the built-in rules of biology (described in Mechanics below). The player can adjust some parameters either at the start or during the run (depending on the mode) 鈥?for instance, introducing more food, toggling an environmental factor 鈥?to see how it affects the population. When the throng meets the requirement of the win-condition, the simulation stops and the player wins the game.

flowchart TD
  
  %% Throng: Evolution - High-level Loop

  A[Set up conditions<br/>initial genes, resources, modifiers] --> B[Run simulation]

  %% Simulation phase (autonomous lifecycle)
  B --> M1[Creatures move]
  M1 --> M2[Eat / gain energy]
  M2 --> M3[Reproduce if threshold met]
  M3 --> M4[Die from age or starvation]

  %% Observe outcomes
  M4 --> C[Observe outcomes<br/>charts, telemetry, traits]

  %% Optional intervention
  C --> D{Player intervenes?}
  D -- Yes --> E[Adjust parameters<br/>e.g., add food, toggle factor]
  E --> B

  D -- No --> F[Next generation evolves<br/>selection & mutation]

  %% Win condition
  F --> G{Win-condition met?}
  G -- Yes --> H[Stop simulation<br/>Player wins]
  G -- No --> B

Gameplay & Mechanics

flowchart TD A[Parameter Setup] --> B[Run Simulation] B --> C[Thronglets Move | Gather | Reproduce | Die] C --> D[Telemetry Updates & Charts] D --> E{Player Adjusts?} E -->|Yes| A E -->|No| F[Observe Long-Term Evolution]
The game world provides the environmental context in which evolution occurs. It consists of a bounded area that contains resource patches (food sources). Each resource patch has a certain amount of food that regenerates over time. The total amount of available food effectively creates a carrying capacity for the creature population 鈥?there is only so much energy to go around. If the population grows too large for the environment to support, individuals will start to starve. This models the classic population dynamics concept: resources limit population growth[2].

Traits and Genetics

鈥he creatures (let鈥檚 call them 鈥淭hronglets鈥? are the agents of evolution in the game. Each thronglet has a set of heritable traits (genes) that affect its survival and reproductive success. In the current design, there are five key traits, each corresponding to a gene:

Speed: Determines how fast the creature can move around the environment. A higher speed helps a thronglet reach food patches more quickly, which is advantageous if food is scarce or competition is high. However, speed comes at a cost (see Metabolism below).

Metabolic Rate: This governs how fast the creature uses up energy (food). A higher metabolism means the creature must eat more frequently to avoid starvation. There is an implicit trade-off between Speed and Metabolism in our design 鈥?typically, creatures that move faster also consume energy faster. Thus, being swift can be a liability if food is sparse, reflecting real-life trade-offs (e.g. a shrew must eat almost constantly due to its high metabolism).

Lifespan: How long the creature can live (in simulation time) if it doesn鈥檛 die from other causes. A longer lifespan increases the chance to find food and reproduce over the creature鈥檚 life, but long-lived individuals might also consume more total resources. Shorter-lived individuals might reproduce earlier (this trait may co-vary with Reproduction cost).

Reproduction Threshold: This trait represents how much energy (food stored) the creature needs in order to reproduce. In nature, organisms often require surplus energy or resources to invest in offspring. In the game, a thronglet must accumulate a certain amount of energy before it can create offspring. A lower reproduction cost means a creature can reproduce more easily (with less food), potentially leading to more offspring when resources are limited. But if reproduction cost is too low, it might reproduce so often that it depletes its energy and dies or floods the environment with too many offspring that then starve (another interesting scenario to observe!).

Gathering Efficiency: How effectively the creature harvests food from a patch per unit time. Some thronglets might be better foragers 鈥?for example, one with higher gather rate can extract food quickly from a patch, whereas a lower rate means it eats slowly. This can determine how well a creature does in competition when multiple individuals swarm the same food source.

All these traits are genetic 鈥?meaning they are passed 鈥?spring with slight modifications (mutations). In the game鈥檚 UI, players can view the population averages of each trait at any time (e.g. 鈥淎verage speed = 5.2 units, Average lifespan = 20s, 鈥︹€?. This is a critical learning feature: as the game progresses, players can see these averages shift, which is essentially observing evolution. For example, if the environment suddenly has less food, one might notice the average metabolic rate of the population decreases over generations (because high-metabolism creatures died off, leaving lower-metabolism ones reproducing more). By quantifying traits, the game gives a concrete window into the otherwise abstract concept of 鈥渁llele frequencies鈥?or trait distributions changing over time.

Reproduction & Mutation

Key points about the reproduction system:

Age and Reproduction Timing: Each creature has an internal timer or age. It may attempt reproduction after a certain maturity time and then again after each interval (provided it has accumulated the required energy). This ensures that not all creatures reproduce synchronously, and it creates overlapping generations (much like real populations).

Cost of Reproduction: As mentioned, reproducing deducts a chunk of the creature鈥檚 stored energy (simulating the investment of calories into an offspring). After reproducing, the parent might be left with low energy and need to feed again before it can reproduce a second time. This can sometimes lead to death if the environment is harsh 鈥?e.g. a creature reproduces and then starves because it gave its last energy to the offspring. Such events can provoke discussion about life-history strategies (should one reproduce as soon as possible, or wait to gather more energy?).

Offspring Inheritance: The offspring starts with trait values equal to the parent鈥檚, plus a random delta from mutation. For example, if a parent has speed 5.0, the child might have speed 5.2 or 4.7, etc. The range of possible mutation is small (perhaps 卤5-10% of the trait value), so changes are gradual, reflecting real 鈥?

Game Scene

speed 5.0, speed 5.2, speed 4.9, speed 5.1, speed 5.7, speed 4.6, speed 4.7 (figure labels preserved as-is)

Survival and Natural Selection Mechanics

Not all creatures will survive in the game 鈥?and that鈥檚 by design. Natural selection occurs as a emergent result of the game鈥檚 survival rules. The rules are straightforward: a thronglet dies if it runs out of energy (starves) or if it reaches the end of its lifespan. In advanced scenarios, death can also occur by predation (if a predator catches a prey creature). The combination of these rules with the environment and traits leads to differential survival:

Starvation and Competition

Each creature is constantly using energy (due to metabolism). It must eat from resource patches to refill its energy reserves. If many creatures are competing for limited patches, not everyone will get enough. Those individuals with traits that let them secure food (e.g. faster movement to get there first, or better efficiency extracting food, or simply needing less food due to low metabolism) have a higher chance of surviving. Slower or high-metabolism individuals are at a disadvantage in a food-scarce scenario and will likely die off first when food runs out. This directly demonstrates 鈥渢he struggle for existence鈥?that Darwin described 鈥?many are born, fewer survive, typically those with advantageous traits relative to the current environment[6]. Players can observe, for example, that after a few rounds of scarcity, the population is full of the more efficient eaters and the ones that could survive on little food. This is natural selection in action: the trait (low metabolism, say) becomes more common in the next generation because the individuals with high metabolism didn鈥檛 survive to reproduce.

Lifespan and Generational Turnover

Creatures will eventually die of old age even if they have food. This ensures that even in a rich environment, there is turnover and opportunity for the next generation. Longer lifespan is generally beneficial because it gives more opportunities to reproduce, but if a creature鈥檚 lifespan is long but it never gets to reproduce (perhaps due to high food demands), that trait won鈥檛 propagate. We balance the game such that multiple strategies can play out 鈥?sometimes a 鈥渇ast, reproduce early, die young鈥?strategy might leave more offspring than a 鈥渟low and steady鈥?strategy, depending on context, which can lead to interesting discussions.

Taken together, these mechanics create a feedback loop: creatures with favorable traits survive longer -> they reproduce more -> their genes (traits) spread in the population; unfavorable traits get weeded out (those individuals die before reproducing). The player doesn鈥檛 need to be told this in abstract terms; they will see it happen. However, the game does provide explanatory pop-up tips at key moments to reinforce the point. By coupling the mechanics with explanatory text, we ensure the educational content is explicit.

Conclusion

Throng: Evolution is more than just a game 鈥?it is an interactive learning experience grounded in scientific research and pedagogy. By simulating an evolutionary 鈥渟urvival game,鈥?it tackles known learning challenges in biology education: it makes abstract concepts concrete, addresses common misconceptions (like what 鈥渇ittest鈥?really means), and engages players in active problem-solving. The design of the game leverages the strengths of serious games 鈥?motivation, immersion, immediate feedback 鈥?while consciously incorporating features to keep the focus on learning outcomes. Through gameplay, players gain a better understanding of natural selection and species evolution in a memorable way. They witness first-hand why survival of the fittest truly means survival of those best adapted to their environment, not necessarily the physically strongest. They also see how environmental constraints (resource limits, carrying capacity) and random variation shape the destiny of populations. In essence, the game brings Darwin鈥檚 principles to life on the screen: variation, overproduction, competition, and differential survival are not just words in a textbook, but dynamic processes the player can observe and influence.

Early testing of the game (informal observations in a classroom setting) has shown high engagement 鈥?students often react with surprise and excitement when 鈥渆volution鈥?happens in front of them (鈥淟ook, all the fast ones died off!鈥?followed by discussions on why that occurred). This kind of enthusiasm is exactly what is needed in science education, where student interest can sometimes be a limiting factor. While engagement is clearly boosted, we remain mindful of ensuring genuine learning takes place. The integrated explanations and the design of reflection prompts (either in-game or via an instructor鈥檚 guide) aim to solidify the knowledge gained. This aligns with research indicating that games need to be complemented by debriefing or reflection to maximize learning gains[10]. In conclusion, Throng: Evolution demonstrates how a carefully crafted serious game can serve as an effective educational tool. It uses the power of play to illuminate one of science鈥檚 most important ideas. By guiding a virtual species through the trials of survival, players come away with a deeper intuition for natural selection 鈥?an intuition that we hope will translate to better understanding of real-world biology and evolution.

content:
“Every sip could be your last.” A strategy & bluffing tabletop card game where vampires drink, scheme, and survive in a ruined village.

Atmosphere & Hook (click to expand)
The silent village reeks of iron and despair. Once a secret laboratory for humans and vampire hunters, it now lies in ruins, crowded only by abandoned “experiments” — the villagers. Starved vampires gather here to feed. Each sip risks poison, each choice risks your rivals. Higher the risk, higher the profit — until it kills you.

Partial Portfolio PDF

click here

Objectives

  • 2 Players: First to 50 BP (Blood Points), or make opponent reach 15 TOX (Toxins).
  • 3–6 Players: First to 60 BP, or last vampire standing (others eliminated at 20 TOX).
  • Creative Mode: Customize BP/TOX thresholds and NGCA ratios to tune difficulty.

Core Ideas (NGCA • Chain Drinking • Designate)

  • NGCA stack decides blood type per villager: N (Normal), G (Garlic), C (Convert), A (Antidote).
  • Chain Drinking increases BP each sip (1, 2, 3, …) but if the stack judges Vampire (V) or Garlic (G), you take TOX equal to the current sip count and the chain stops.
  • Designate lets you push the current sip to another player (they draw 1–3 cards before judgment), sharing risk/reward.
  • Forfeit trades your sip for 2 Operation or 2 Item cards — tempo vs. information vs. control.

Concept art — the ruined vampire village.

Cards & Setup

Category Name Effect
Operation Normal (N) Baseline judgment card (human blood path).
Operation Convert (C) Shifts blood toward Vampire (poison to vampires).
Operation Antidote (A) Neutralizes Convert (C−A decreases).
Operation Garlic (G) Instantly Garlic blood: take TOX, villager eliminated.
Item Spy Peek at a villager’s stacked card(s).
Item Detox Reduce your TOX by 1.
Item Slay Scavenge eliminated villagers / profit from V blood.
Item Blood Loot Drain 4 BP from another player; +1 TOX to you.
Initial Setup (click to expand)
  • Villagers: Use 2 × players face-down as the blood source pile.
  • Items: Each player starts with 2 random Item cards.
  • Operations: Shuffle NGCA into a common draw pile.
  • Decide starting player randomly.

Operation & Item samples (NGCA + utilities).

Turn Sequence (Booklet Flow)

flowchart TD A[Turn Start] --> B{Use 1 Item?} B -- Yes --> B1[Resolve Item] --> C B -- No --> C[Blood Drinking Phase] C --> D[Choose a Villager] D --> E[Draw 2 Operation Cards -> Stack on that Villager] E --> F{Blood Type Judgment} F -- H (Human) --> G[Gain BP = sip count] G --> H{Continue Chain?} H -- Continue --> E H -- Stop --> Z[End of Blood Phase] F -- V (Vampire) --> I[Gain TOX = sip count; Chain ends] F -- G (Garlic) --> J[Gain TOX = sip count; Villager eliminated] Z --> K{Alternative Action} K -- Designate --> L[Other player draws 1-3 then judge] --> Z2[End Turn] K -- Forfeit --> M[Gain 2 Operation OR 2 Item] --> Z2
Judgment Rule (click to expand)

Blood Type Judgment from the visible NGCA stack:

  • If Garlic (G) appears → Garlic blood.
  • Else compute C−A: if C−A ≥ 2 → Vampire blood.
  • Otherwise → Human blood.

Chain Drinking (unbounded):

  • 1st sip: if H → +1 BP; if V/G → +1 TOX and stop.
  • 2nd sip: if H → +2 BP; if V/G → +2 TOX and stop.
  • …
  • n-th sip: if H → +n BP; if V/G → +n TOX and stop.

Risk ramps up with each sip; a single G/V flips all greed into TOX.

Risk vs Reward

  • Greedy: Keep sipping to ramp BP fast → explosive TOX risk.
  • Cautious: Early stop or Designate to others → safer tempo but slower points.
  • Forfeit: Trade a sip for card advantage (operations or items) and information.

Chain-Drinking: BP rewards ramp 1→2→3…, but a V/G hit gives TOX equal to current sip count.

Designate Details (click to expand)

  • You may assign the current sip to another player.

  • The designated player chooses to draw 1–3 Operation cards before judgment:

    • Draw 3: bold and risky; highest chance to trigger V/G.
    • Draw 1: safer probe.

  • Often used when the stack feels on the knife-edge (C−A = 1/0).

Item Effects (Full Text)

Spy
  • On your turn: peek 1 stacked card of a chosen villager.
  • When designated to drink: you may use Spy before drawing to preview risk.
  • Character variants may allow peeking 2 cards.
Detox
  • On your turn: reduce your TOX by 1.
  • When designated: may be used to neutralize partial toxins.
Slay
  • Target a villager eliminated by G: gain all hand cards (Operation/Item) from that villager’s stack.
  • Target a villager judged V: gain +2 BP but take +1 TOX.
Blood Loot
  • Use on another player: they −4 BP, you +1 TOX.
  • Usable once per turn, during your turn.

Special Rules

Villager Resupply
When all villagers have been judged V or G, immediately add +1 new villager from reserve.
Pushing V-blood Villagers
Players may agree whether revealed V-blood villagers can be pushed (designated) to others — allowed by default.
Garlic Restriction
Villagers judged G are eliminated and cannot be drunk by anyone.

Characters & Skills

Character Ability
Reaper Gain +2 BP when using Slay.
Detective Spy 2 cards when using Spy.
Nurse Gain +1 BP with Blood Loot and do not take its +1 TOX.
Guardian First G against you is auto-neutralized.
Scholar Draw +1 Operation card at the start of your turns.

Playable vampire cast in semi-realistic oil-paint style.

Physical Deck Composition (Finite Cards)

To keep tension with finite physical stock:

Card Count Ratio
Normal (N) 40 8
Garlic (G) 15 3
Convert (C) 40 8
Antidote (A) 25 5
Total 120 8:3:8:5
Shuffle & Reset Rules (click to expand)
  • Slay on G-blood: When a player uses Slay on a G-blood villager, shuffle all discards + remaining draw pile back into a fresh Operations pile; that player also gains +1 extra Item (reward for risk).
  • Major Reset: If the table stalls with no H outcomes on the field, refresh all villager slots, shuffle all discards into a new draw pile, and restart the deck cycle.

Playtesting & Iteration

Early prototype used pre-placing operation cards on villagers — functional but too deterministic. After feedback, we redesigned to on-turn draws and Chain-Drinking:

“This feels like gambling. Every extra sip makes my heart race.” “Finally, there’s real tension between greed and caution.”

Peer playtests — tension spikes under chain decisions.

Online playtests — tension spikes under chain decisions.

Quickstart (One Page)

  1. Choose villager → draw 2 Operation cards to that villager’s stack.
  2. Judge blood by NGCA rule (G → Garlic; else C−A≥2 → Vampire; else Human).
  3. If Human: gain BP = sip count, then continue or stop.
  4. If Vampire/Garlic: take TOX = sip count, chain ends; G also eliminates the villager.
  5. Optionally Designate a sip to someone else (they draw 1–3), or Forfeit to draw 2 Op / 2 Item.
  6. End Turn.

Videos

Online Playtest Version/PDF design Download & Source

  • GitHub: https://github.com/GeraAer/SilentFeast
  • Seperate PDF: click here

Visual Style

The game adopts a semi-realistic oil-painting look with dark, moody tones. Thick brushstrokes add depth while keeping readability for tabletop icons.

Dark tones and hand-painted textures support the gothic atmosphere.
